title: Bill Ackman's Bold Bet: Snapping Up Netflix, NYSE Owner Amidst Market Chaos
summary: Billionaire investor Bill Ackman's Pershing Square fund capitalized on recent market turbulence by strategically adding six new prominent stocks, including streaming giant Netflix and market operator ICE, to its portfolio. This aggressive, deep-value approach signals Ackman's belief in the long-term resilience of established market leaders despite current volatility.
content:
Bill Ackman, the often-contrarian billionaire hedge fund manager at Pershing Square, clearly isn't one to shy away from a bumpy ride. As the stock market navigated a tumultuous "roller coaster" last quarter, Ackman’s fund wasn’t just observing; it was actively seizing opportunity, strategically snapping up six new, prominent positions. This aggressive move, revealed in his latest quarterly letter to investors, underscores a familiar Ackman playbook: pounce when others hesitate.

Among the standout additions are streaming behemoth Netflix and Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), the powerful parent company of the New York Stock Exchange. Investing in Netflix, which has seen its share price fluctuate dramatically in recent times, signals a deep belief in the long-term resilience and ultimate dominance of its core business model, despite competitive pressures and subscriber growth concerns. Meanwhile, a stake in ICE represents a shrewd bet on the fundamental infrastructure of global finance, an essential service regardless of market ups and downs. These aren't speculative startups; they're established titans, suggesting Ackman sees considerable intrinsic value overlooked by short-term market anxieties.

Ackman’s investment philosophy typically zeroes in on high-quality companies with strong competitive moats that are trading below their intrinsic value. His latest shopping spree during a period of widespread market uncertainty aligns perfectly with this deep-value, activist approach. It suggests a conviction that certain market leaders have been unfairly punished, creating a window for significant long-term gains for those with the patience and capital to weather current volatility.

This series of bold maneuvers from one of Wall Street's most watched investors could be interpreted as a potential signal for broader market confidence, or at least a vote of confidence in specific, fundamentally strong sectors. For retail and institutional investors alike, Ackman’s latest portfolio adjustments offer a glimpse into where a seasoned hand is finding overlooked value, providing a compelling narrative amidst the market's ongoing ebb and flow.
keyTakeaways: Bill Ackman's Pershing Square fund took six new stock positions during recent market turbulence.
Key additions include streaming giant Netflix and Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), owner of the NYSE.
Ackman's strategy reflects a deep-value approach, targeting established companies he believes are undervalued due to short-term market anxieties.
author: sobrient@insider.com (Samuel O'Brient)

title: The Musk Effect? S&P 500 CEO Pay Soars to Record Highs
summary: Executive compensation packages across the S&P 500 saw a significant surge in 2025, with average CEO pay, even excluding Elon Musk, jumping 21% to $22.8 million. This dramatic rise is attributed in part to the growing influence of "Musk-inspired" compensation models, which tie massive payouts to aggressive performance milestones.
content:
The executive suites of America’s largest companies are seeing a truly stratospheric rise in compensation, even as the broader economy navigates its own set of challenges. In 2025, the average pay for chief executives across the S&P 500 surged an astonishing 21% to a staggering $22.8 million. What makes this figure even more eye-popping is that it excludes the often-anomalous pay packages of figures like Elon Musk, the visionary behind Tesla and SpaceX.

This dramatic ascent isn't merely an organic rise; analysts point to a growing trend of "Musk-inspired" compensation plans spreading throughout corporate America. These aren't your grandfather's quarterly bonuses. Instead, they often involve complex, long-term equity grants tied to incredibly ambitious performance benchmarks – think moonshot market caps, revolutionary product launches, or aggressive growth targets. The idea, proponents argue, is to align executive incentives directly with monumental shareholder value creation, mirroring the audacious goals set by leaders like Musk.

While designed to spur innovation and bold strategic moves, this new era of executive compensation raises crucial questions. Is this a sustainable model for rewarding leadership, or does it further exacerbate the widening chasm between executive pay and the average worker’s wages? Critics contend that such gargantuan payouts, even when tied to performance, can detach corporate leadership from the realities faced by their employees and customers.

The influx of these performance-heavy packages reflects a changing corporate landscape, where investors demand not just incremental growth but disruptive, transformative value. Companies are seemingly betting big on their leaders to deliver, offering unprecedented incentives for unprecedented results. Whether this trend continues its upward trajectory or faces a backlash from shareholders and the public remains to be seen, but for now, it's clear that the path to the top is more lucrative than ever.
keyTakeaways: Average S&P 500 CEO compensation, excluding Elon Musk, hit a record $22.8 million in 2025, marking a 21% increase.
This surge is significantly influenced by the spread of "Musk-inspired" compensation plans, which tie massive equity grants to ambitious, long-term performance targets.
The rise in executive pay sparks debate on its sustainability, its impact on income inequality, and whether it truly aligns executive incentives with value creation.
author: Reuters
